issues.legal_issue: When execution of an earlier will is admitted but its revocation by later wills is alleged, the party asserting revocation must establish the later wills.
material_facts: The execution of the earlier will was admitted.
The appellants relied on two later wills to claim that the earlier will had been revoked.
The respondent disputed the later wills, and the courts found that they had not been proved.
issues.conclusion: The earlier will did not require proof of its execution because its execution was admitted; the appellants had to prove the later wills on which they relied to establish revocation, and they failed to do so.
issues.legal_principle: The party relying on a will must prove its execution when that execution is denied. Where execution is not denied, the party relying on it need not prove it. The Court approved the First Appellate Court’s application of this principle.

rule.if: will_based_claim and earlier_will_execution_admitted and revocation_by_later_will_claimed and later_wills_not_proved

predicates.will_based_claim: A party relies on a will to establish testamentary rights or to establish that another will was revoked.
predicates.earlier_will_execution_admitted: The opposing party does not dispute that the earlier will was executed.
predicates.revocation_by_later_will_claimed: A party asserts that a later will revoked the earlier will.
predicates.later_wills_not_proved: The party relying on the later wills fails to establish their execution.

issues.definition: When execution of an earlier will is admitted and the later wills relied on to claim its revocation are not proved, the earlier will remains unrevoked.

issues.legal_issue: A will required to be attested must be proved through the prescribed execution and attestation evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on two later wills, whose execution the respondent disputed.
No attesting witness to either later will was examined, although attesting witnesses were alive and capable of being called.
The courts found that the later wills had not been proved.
issues.conclusion: The later wills were not proved because the required statutory proof of execution and attestation was not supplied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires a will to be signed or marked by the testator, or signed by another person in the testator’s presence and at the testator’s direction, and attested by at least two witnesses in the prescribed manner. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, explains these requirements; the Court also referred to Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, (2006) 13 SCC 433, and Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, as following that law.

rule.if: will_based_claim and execution_contested and attesting_witness_available and no_attesting_witness_examined

predicates.will_based_claim: A party relies on a will to establish testamentary rights or to establish that another will was revoked.
predicates.execution_contested: The opposing party disputes that the will was executed.
predicates.attesting_witness_available: At least one attesting witness is alive and capable of giving evidence.
predicates.no_attesting_witness_examined: The party relying on the will does not call an available attesting witness to prove its execution.

issues.definition: If a party relies on a disputed will and does not call an available attesting witness, the will is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances is not accepted as the testator’s last will unless the propounder satisfactorily removes those suspicions.
material_facts: The later wills were allegedly made while the testator was unwell and only a short time before his death.
They were allegedly made while the testator was staying at the residence of the person who benefited under them, although that person had received no provision under the earlier will.
The witnesses to the later wills were strangers to the family, and the wills surfaced only when a defence was filed in the suit.
The appellants did not remove the suspicious circumstances identified by the courts.
issues.conclusion: The appellants failed to discharge the heavy burden of removing the suspicious circumstances, so the later wills could not be accepted as the testator’s last wills.
issues.legal_principle: Under H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, circumstances such as a weakened or debilitated testator, insufficient evidence of mental capacity, an unnatural or unfair disposition, or a bequest not shown to result from the testator’s free will may raise suspicion. The propounder bears a heavy burden to remove legitimate suspicions before the will can be accepted. The Court also cited Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, (2006) 13 SCC 433, and Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, as following the governing law on proof of wills.

predicates.will_based_claim: A party relies on a will to establish testamentary rights or to establish that another will was revoked.
predicates.suspicious_execution_context: The circumstances surrounding execution or the terms of the will raise legitimate doubts about whether it reflects the testator’s free and genuine wishes.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_remove_suspicion: The party relying on the will does not satisfactorily dispel the legitimate doubts surrounding it.

issues.definition: If a party relies on a will, its circumstances raise legitimate doubts, and the party fails to dispel those doubts, the will is not accepted as the testator’s last will.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not disturb supported factual findings in a second appeal when no substantial question of law was erroneously decided.
material_facts: The First Appellate Court found that the later wills had not been proved, and the High Court affirmed that finding.
The Supreme Court found no substantial question of law that had been erroneously decided by the First Appellate Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right not to interfere with the findings in the second appeal, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the High Court correctly declined to interfere in the second appeal because no substantial question of law had been erroneously decided by the First Appellate Court.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.supported_factual_findings: The lower appellate court made factual findings supported by its assessment of the evidence.
predicates.no_erroneous_substantial_law_decision: No substantial question of law was erroneously decided by the lower appellate court.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, supported factual findings should not be disturbed when no substantial question of law was erroneously decided.
